summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted API for chat/text gen focused on streaming behavior, parameter controls, and retry/backoff patterns. Customer (GreenArc) is evaluating a pilot to replace an in-house GPU inference path for low-latency analytics assistants. Key asks: latency targets (p95 < 250ms for short queries), data controls/SOC2, and cost estimate for 100k monthly active users.
topics: console walkthrough: routing and Optimize suggestions
transcript:
Header: Date/Time: 2027-10-25 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (GreenArc Eng Lead), Tom Reynolds (GreenArc CTO), Aisha Khan (GreenArc SRE)
Artifacts shared: console tour recording link: https://redwood.example/demo/ff-20271025, pilot checklist sheet: https://docs.example/greenarc-pilot

00:00 Maya Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a quick 45-ish minute run the idea is live demo first, then q and a and next steps. Luis is on the technical side. does that timing ok?
00:10 Priya Nair: yeah fine for us, thanks, quick note we have Tom and Aisha here for infra/security q's.
00:18 Luis Ortega: cool i'll kick it off with a short console tour then we'll show streaming examples and some failure modes, sorry for the slight echo, my headset...
00:32 Maya Chen: and i'll surface pricing and pilot options at the end, nothing final but a starting point.
01:05 Luis Ortega: alright i'm in the console. first, model selection — we show a medium-latency variant and a cheaper quantized variant. important for streaming: we keep a small chunk size, continuous KV cache reuse so short-turn queries get sub-200ms tail in many cases. "KV cache" often transcribed as "K V cache" in notes, apologies.
01:40 Tom Reynolds: can you explain how the streaming actually works? are you sending partial tokens? what's the client contract?
01:53 Luis Ortega: yes, streaming is server-sent events style — you get partial tokens as they are decoded. client receives chunked deltas plus a final event. we also expose the "delta" token stream and a final "done" event for latency-sensitive UI. from an implementation side we support both WebSocket and http/2 streams; examples are in the SDK.
02:20 Aisha Khan: what about ordering guarantees? if a worker fails mid-stream do we re-stream from the start?
02:34 Luis Ortega: good question. we do short reconnects with resume tokens — we keep a KV cache pointer and the client can request resume from the last acknowledged token. for longer failures we fall back to a full retry with idempotency token so you either get a clean re-run or a gracefully degraded shorter response.
03:05 Priya Nair: resume tokens — is that automatic or something we need to wire?
03:10 Luis Ortega: it's automatic in our SDKs; if you call raw REST you can pass the resume token we return in the stream meta. there is also a built-in exponential backoff policy default: 500ms initial, *2, capped at 8s, with jitter. you can override on request or set a per-route policy in the console.
03:42 Tom Reynolds: latency targets — our p95 goal for short queries is under 250ms. what kind of real numbers do you see?
03:50 Luis Ortega: depends on model and region. for a small short-turn model on hosted with regional routing we commonly see p50 ~60-80ms, p95 around 180-280ms for 16-64 token responses. for longer outputs p95 obviously increases. We showed a latency profile in the console: per-route time breakdowns (network, queue, decode). note that continuous batching can add 10-30ms at high throughput, but reduces cost per token significantly.
04:30 Maya Chen: customers often choose a hybrid: low-latency routes pinned to faster variants and background tasks on cheaper quantized models. Optimize will recommend that split after a few days of telemetry.
05:02 Priya Nair: okay i want to see the SDK example for streaming.
05:08 Luis Ortega: switching to the live code sandbox. here's a node snippet, we set streaming:true, model: "redwood-small-v1-stream-variant" and we pass an idempotency_token for safety. watch the console — i'll trigger a short prompt.
05:46 (audio cue)
06:00 Luis Ortega: you can see partial chunks come in, then final. sometimes transcription shows token fragments like "--ing" or punctuation on next chonk, clients should accumulate.
06:30 Priya Nair: if stream breaks halfway what is best practice? do you re-render or show a spinner?
06:38 Luis Ortega: best practice we recommend: show partial text as it arrives, keep an ephemeral buffer keyed by the idempotency/resume token, and when reconnecting attempt a resume first; if resume fails, fetch full response using the same idempotency token and then replace the UI content. that avoids duplication or partial-overlaps.
07:10 Tom Reynolds: how do retries affect billing? if you retry and keyboard fetch full response are you double billed?
07:20 Maya Chen: billing is per-token rendered; we have smart detection to avoid double-charging for resumes in most cases. if a hard retry occurs we charge for the completed output only — short internal replays used for resume do not bill the customer. we'll share the exact billing logic in the pilot doc.
07:45 Aisha Khan: we need data residency and log retention controls — can't send certain PII to external systems. do you retain prompts?
07:53 Maya Chen: hosted default is ephemeral unless you opt-in to long retention. for the pilot we can disable persistent logs and enable customer-side filtering. SOC 2 and ISO stuff is in the attestation pack i'll share. we also offer Private deployment if you need VPC/on-prem.
08:20 Priya Nair: what about encryption keys?
08:23 Maya Chen: we support customer-managed KMS for Private + Dedicated tiers; hosted offers server-side encryption and HSM-backed key material for enterprise customers. details in the security pack.
08:45 Luis Ortega: pivoting back to params: temperature, top_p, max_tokens — these affect streaming behavior and token counts. lower temperature tends to finish faster in many heuristics. Also "stop" sequences can cut tokens early — useful for latency-sensitive responses.
09:25 Priya Nair: can Escape tokens cause partial streams to flush weirdly?
09:30 Luis Ortega: sometimes you see a partial token at flush boundary, SDKs handle recombination. also we recommend sending explicit stop tokens rather than relying on context truncation.
10:05 Tom Reynolds: can we throttle or limit concurrency? during spikes we can't have runaway costs.
10:12 Maya Chen: yes per-api-key rate limits, per-deployment quotas, and console-level concurrency caps. we also support burst policies: keep certain band reserved for your critical routes.
10:38 Aisha Khan: how do you handle backpressure from GPU pools? if jobs queue do you expose queue length?
10:45 Luis Ortega: Console shows queue length and estimated wait time. routing policies let you direct critical low-latency calls to reserved pools. fallback policy can route to a cheaper variant with shorter context to avoid long waits.
11:12 Priya Nair: show us retries in action for a failed decode.
11:18 Luis Ortega: ok i'll artificially inject an error. (pause) you see the client reconnect, it requests resume with token x, small delta continued then final. if resume can't be applied you get a 409 retry recommended with idempotency header. in the SDK the flow is automatic.
11:55 Tom Reynolds: is there a way to run A/B for quality vs cost? we might want to compare quantized vs full float for same prompt set.
12:05 Luis Ortega: yes — console supports canary rollouts and A/B experiments per route. Optimize will surface quantization recommendations and expected cost/quality tradeoffs after analyzing evals. you can also pin model tags to routes for easy compare.
12:40 Priya Nair: what about token accounting? we have a distorted prompt amplification with templates. can you show cost per route?
12:50 Maya Chen: in Console -> Billing -> Per-route tokens you can see per-token breakdown and per-token latency. Optimize will suggest batching/caching and expected savings.
13:15 Luis Ortega: small demo of prefix caching: if you have repeated system prompt segments we can cache kv-prefix and skip recomputation which saves tokens and latency. we'll show a cache hit example now.
13:45 (demo plays)
14:05 Priya Nair: Hmm the cache hit looks good. how long is the cache kept?
14:12 Luis Ortega: cache TTL's configurable — default 15 minutes for hosted but can be tuned. for Dedicated you can set longer retention and warm caches.
14:35 Tom Reynolds: for our traffic pattern many queries are short Q/A under 20 tokens, but we see spikes every hour. what configuration would you recommend?
14:45 Luis Ortega: reserve a low-latency pool for critical routes, set batching window very small (like 2-5ms) to avoid aggregation latency, enable caching for repeated prefixes, and set a burst policy for occasional spikes. in Optimize we can produce a recommended config based on the sample traffic you provide.
15:10 Aisha Khan: security — can we audit who called what model and see per-token trace?
15:18 Maya Chen: yes audit logs with per-request metadata are available (enterprise retention options). we also support SSO SAML and RBAC controls to limit who can deploy routes.
15:40 Priya Nair: ok can you summarise pilot scope and what you need from us?
15:45 Maya Chen: sure — pilot scope: 2-week bench then 4-week production-like pilot: we need sample prompt set (10k messages), traffic profile (qps distribution), latency targets, and a contact for entitlements. deliverables: pilot SLO dashboard, latency/cost report, and a recommendation doc from Optimize.
16:20 Priya Nair: voice check — our timeline target is mid-november for start. is that feasible?
16:28 Maya Chen: yes if we get artifacts by Oct 28 we can slot a pilot for mid-Nov.
16:40 (questions back and forth)
20:00 Tom Reynolds: do you do throttling based on tokens or requests?
20:06 Luis Ortega: both — you can set token-based caps or req-based caps per API key.
20:30 Priya Nair: edge cases: what happens if a client keeps reconnecting and never completes?
20:38 Luis Ortega: there's idle timeout and ephemeral session cleanup; long-running sockets get reclaimed and resume tokens expire after 5 minutes by default to avoid leaks, configurable in Dedicated/Private.
21:10 Aisha Khan: if we want to run the bench on our data, can we use a private agent or does it hit your hosted fleet?
21:20 Maya Chen: pilot can run on hosted with data-control settings (no persistent logs) or on Dedicated where pools are reserved to you. Private is also possible but adds onboarding time. we'll outline tradeoffs.
22:05 Priya Nair: any gotchas for prompt punctuation or stop tokens that often break our front end?
22:12 Luis Ortega: yes, avoid trailing partial stop tokens that are split by streaming chunk boundaries; rely on SDK recombine or submit the stop as a separate earlier token. small UI changes can avoid jerkiness.
23:00 Tom Reynolds: what about long responses >1024 tokens? how do you stream and bill?
23:08 Luis Ortega: streamed, yes. billing counts tokens produced. we recommend streaming large outputs to the client incrementally and using chunked storage if you need to persist. there is also partial-save hooks in the SDK.
24:00 (brief pause)
24:12 Priya Nair: can you show Optimize suggestions now?
24:20 Luis Ortega: switching to Optimize tab — the product suggests batching window, model variant per route, and quantization points. here it suggests moving cold-path logs to quantized variant saving ~45% token-cost. these are heuristic at first but become precise after telemetry.
25:00 Priya Nair: i like the recommended split of live assistant + background summarizer.
25:15 Maya Chen: same pattern many customers adopt.
25:30 Tom Reynolds: one more security question — do you do data plane encryption in transit and at rest?
25:36 Maya Chen: yes TLS in transit and AES-256 at rest; enterprise keys via KMS for Dedicated/Private.
26:00 Aisha Khan: we may need to sign a DPA and add specific clauses. who handles that?
26:06 Maya Chen: our contracts team handles it; i'll loop in legal after this call.
26:30 (Luis runs a short failover show)
27:00 Luis Ortega: here's a scenario: sudden pool OOM — routing policy triggers fallback to next compatible model, client gets a slightly shorter response but service remains available. fallback policy is configurable: strict fail vs degrade vs queue.
28:00 Tom Reynolds: so graceful degradation is built in, good.
28:22 Priya Nair: what metrics will you expose in pilot?
28:30 Maya Chen: per-request latency histograms, tokens per call, cache hit ratio, queue length, and error rates. We'll also include a cost-forecast widget.
29:05 Priya Nair: ok, next steps recap?
29:10 Maya Chen: we'll send pricing + SOW draft, security pack, and a console recording. Luis will prepare the benchmark plan and we request prompt set and traffic profile from Priya.
29:30 Priya Nair: noted. I'll pull together the prompt set and sync with Tom/Aisha.
30:00 Tom Reynolds: any open concerns? I want to know how you guarantee p95 with noisy neighbors.
30:10 Luis Ortega: reserved pools and routing policy. for hosted we offer a dedicated-reserved option (Dedicated) when strict p95 is required. otherwise soft reservations and burst caps help.
31:00 Aisha Khan: can we get a short run of 10k messages tomorrow for a smoke?
31:07 Maya Chen: yes we can arrange a 24-hour bench. Luis will own the checklist.
31:25 Priya Nair: thanks, that helps.
31:40 (wrap up)
31:50 Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll email the doc bundle and a calendar invite for pilot kickoff once we have the prompt set. expected kickoff mid-nov if artifacts arrive on time.
32:05 Priya Nair: thanks Maya, thanks Luis.
32:10 Tom Reynolds: thanks everyone.

Notes: voice transcript had some mislabels (Speaker 1 from GreenArc intern). occasional ASR errors: "quantized" heard as "quantisation" and "K V cache" spacing. action items recorded above.
